utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I believe the B/C/S is coming on the English channel. I don't know if that's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm getting the nod that it's been corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dzakula, you are reminded that you are still bound by the declaration that you made yesterday to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth, okay? You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, when we finished yesterday we started to talk about the special session of the RSK that was held at the end of 1992 in Vrbovljani near Okucani and that that session related to --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpretation. I can hear well, but it's not the interpretation. Now I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you hear me now in your own language?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will start my question over again, but I just want to be sure that you understood that the Judge reminded you that you are still bound by the declaration that you made yesterday to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth. Did you understand that from the Judge?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that and I thought that that was it, but I did not hear the interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad now that we've made sure about that. I'll start my question over again. Mr. Dzakula, yesterday when we finished the testimony, we had started to talk about a special session of the RSK that was held at the end of 1992, and I'm going to have to say the name of the village again, in Vrbovljani near Okucani, and that this session related to refugees. Do you recall that testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear, was the session about Serb refugees or Croatian refugees returning to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was discussed were both refugees, Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that you heard that before the meeting occurred of the RSK government, the session, that there had been a meeting with the prime minister and several other ministers in Okucani where they agreed that your proposal would not be adopted. You recall telling us about that meeting yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, who was the prime minister at that time that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Zdravko Zecevic; he was prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Martic was at that meeting, before the session?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Stevo Bogic, deputy prime minister, told me, who returned earlier from that rather short meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, Mr. Whiting. There's a knock somewhere outside here that is disturbing the proceedings. Can someone please check what is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm told it's being checked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you want me to proceed, Your Honour -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know, was Stevo Bogic at that meeting? Had he been at that meeting, himself?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he told me that he was present when they discussed this and that he heard that they had said that nothing would come out of this return action and that I would not be supported in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about what happened at the session itself of the government that dealt with this issue. And I'm particularly interested in, for the purposes of this case, in the discussions about the return of Croatian refugees to the area. Could you tell us what was discussed at the session on this topic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we from Western Slavonia had given a proposal to start the action of returning the refugees, primarily to Western Slavonia and then to other parts of the RSK, and we proposed certain places where this should happen. However, this met with a lack of understanding straight away. It was said that the war had just finished, that wounds were still open, that it was a very delicate issue for the people of the Krajina, and that it was difficult to accept that those people who waged war against us would return to their homes. And I can say that practically it was a majority that thought that way, and certain individuals were very vociferous. However, the idea was that conditions had not been created for the return of refugees and that it could not be started. So that was the conclusion that was reached after a rather lengthy discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you say that your proposal was met with a lack of understanding, that's how it's been translated for us, could you clarify exactly what you mean by that. What do you mean by "lack of understanding"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said that we suggested that return -- the return of refugees should start, they said that this proposal could not be accepted and that refugees could not start returning to the Republic of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And here, to be clear -- I put it in the question, in the original question, but just to be clear, we're talking specifically about Croatian refugees. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about Croat refugees, too, that they should also return to the RSK, to Western Slavonia, but we're also talking about Serb refugees who should return to that part of Western Slavonia who was under the control of the UN and of the Croat authorities. Neither proposal was accepted -- or rather, it was a single proposal concerning the return of refugees both ways, but neither was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So the proposal is -- just to be clear about your answer here, the proposal is about Serb refugees returning to the areas under UN and Croat control and Croat refugees returning to the area under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you said earlier in your -- just a minute or two ago, when you said: "It was difficult" -- that the people who opposed this proposal said that: "It was difficult to accept that those people who waged war against us would return to their homes," who were they talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian refugees who had fled from the RSK during the war, and that is what was meant, how their return could be accepted in the territory of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic speak at this session?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he also said that conditions had not been created for the return. He said that he understood the problem; that's what he said, that he understood the problem and that he understood why I was striving for this return, but that the conditions had not been created for it and that therefore they could not return. Those were his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you agree that the conditions had not been created for the return?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not agree. Because I said that conditions had been created for it in Western Slavonia and that when the Croats returned to the RSK and when the Serbs went to the area that was held by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, support would be rendered and there would also be a balance of fear, so to speak. We would protect refugees who came to our area and we expected the UN to protect Serb refugees who would come to the territory that was under the control of Croatia. We discussed that with the Canadian Battalion, and it could have started. I believe that the climate, if I can put it that way, was already right in our area by then, but the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Those things that you've just said now about the climate being right and how you envisioned how this could happen, did you say those things at the session?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I spoke several times, and I explained that in that area there was already this checkpoint, that is what it was called, where every Thursday members of families would meet up or people who used to live in the same town, about 3.000 of them, they would meet there and talk and then they would go their separate ways. So communication had already started, and I used that by way of an argument, and every time I spoke I said that we can be sure that this process would develop properly. However, there was no support.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this, you testified, was at the end of 1992. Did the position of Milan Martic and the others ever change on the question of the return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, no, because this process had never started. And refugees never returned to the area of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, and the Serbs did not go to the area that we refer to in Western Slavonia where the authorities of the Republic of Croatia exercised control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, yesterday in -- in response to a question, you talked about some crimes that you heard about during 1991. And I just want to go through in a little more detail what you heard with respect to some of the crimes that you mentioned. You mentioned hearing about crimes occurring in Skabrnja in 1991. Can you tell us any more about what you recall having heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before he does so, is it possible to let us know who he heard this from and if that person is going to be called as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I was going to -- I was going to get to that, Your Honour. I was going to ask him what he heard and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even before we can hear the hearsay evidence, I would like to be satisfied - I beg your pardon - that it's going to be confirmed, otherwise we're going to hear a lot of hearsay evidence and it may not be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, hearsay is admissible at the Tribunal and it -- whether it's confirmed or not. Obviously the nature of the testimony, whether it's hearsay or not, will obviously figure in the weight that is given to the testimony. But there's a considerable amount of evidence that will be presented which will be hearsay and which not will necessarily be confirmed in the way that the Court has indicated, that is, that the person will come who actually said it and come and say it. So this is -- under the Rules and under the law of the Tribunal quite a normal way of proceeding, that information is brought out about what people heard at the time. And then of course I will for the Court -- in order to evaluate the evidence and for the Court to determine what kind of weight should be given to the evidence, I will of course follow up on how he heard about it, from whom, and so forth. But I think that the evidence is -- can properly be brought in its form as hearsay evidence before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you able to guide this Court on the probative value of any evidence that's unconfirmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I -- with respect to this issue, I could address that. And of course we will address -- we will -- I'm not sure it's the proper time to do that. But of course we will address the weight that should be given to evidence and why it's important whether it was heard at the time. Why that in itself would have been important. The fact that it was heard at the time actually has significance in terms of notice evidence. So there -- in this case, for example, the fact that it's hearsay I don't think will undermine the evidence; I think it will be very important to the Court's consideration of the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say. I'm not asking you to address the probative value of this specific evidence. I'm asking you as a general rule in this Tribunal where you say hearsay evidence is admissible, I'm saying -- are you able to venture an idea of what probative value is given in this Tribunal to unconfirmed hearsay evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It depends -- it -- I can address that, Your Honour. And it depends completely on the circumstances of the evidence. Sometimes -- and the nature of the issue being discussed and the -- what the witness is able to say and what the Court's evaluation is. There's some hearsay evidence that I would suggest will carry quite a bit of weight and have quite a bit of probative value. There's other hearsay evidence that the Court may determine will not have significant weight. But that -- the whole range is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I -- as you may have gathered from that -- the exchange that I've had with the Chamber, I will -- once I've asked you what you've heard about various matters, I will be interested in following up and making sure I learn and the Chamber can hear where you heard that from and from whom, the best you can remember. But could you tell us first in 1991, what did you hear about crimes committed in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that on the Croatian media, that in Skabrnja a large number of civilians had been killed in actions in which JNA forces had participated as well as the police forces of the Krajina -- or rather, the TO of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you said "police forces of Krajina -- or rather, TO of Krajina." Did -- were you intending to indicate both or one or -- just -- are you able to clarify that at all, whether it was police forces or the TO or both?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you've indicated that you heard this on the Croatian media. Did you hear it from any other source?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, on the Croatian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you hear it at a later time from any other source?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later when I was at the government meeting and when I had contacts with Zdravko Zecevic, he talked about that. He said that there had been crimes, that this had happened. He mentioned Skabrnja. He mentioned some other places, too. I cannot remember exactly which ones he referred to then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And perhaps you've told us, but could you tell us again who Mr. Zecevic was. What position did he hold when you told you this information?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Zecevic was prime minister of the Republic of Serb Krajina, and the two of us travelled to New York in April 1992. We had a lot of time to talk, and he talked about the difficult position of all, notably villages that were ravaged in the war. He mentioned crimes, and in that context he mentioned Skabrnja and some other places, too, but I cannot remember exactly which ones in that context. There was quite a bit of that on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know what municipality Mr. Zecevic was from?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic was from Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was -- do you know if he was in Benkovac during the war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Benkovac in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, to be clear, when you heard about these things in 1991 from the Croatian media, you were, yourself, in -- living in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned yesterday hearing about crimes in Kostajnica. Do you recall what you heard about that in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from the Croat media, too, that there was a lot of fighting in Kostajnica, and that the police and the JNA forces fought against the Croatian police and that many people were arrested. And also that many persons were killed, both civilians and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also mentioned that -- the area of Banija. Can you, first of all, tell us what municipalities are -- to your knowledge, are within that area?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area of Banija are Vrginmost, Petrinja, Glina, Dvor, Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall what you heard in 1991 about crimes in that area?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of those municipalities, in the Croat villages, civilians were killed. That's what I heard from the Croat media. As each municipality fell, from a military point of view, the media were talking about civilians who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally you talked -- you mentioned Dalmatia. Did you hear about crimes committed in Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, likewise. Things were followed in the media. There was a lot of fighting near Zadar, Obrovac, Sibenik, and it was said that in the Croat villages there quite a few people were killed, both Croat policemen and civilians. This was reported on every day, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear about any prisons in the Krajina during 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there was a prison in Knin. I don't know whether it was in the hospital or in the barracks because both locations were mentioned. Also, there were prisons in the police stations, in Benkovac, Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about who was held in these prisons?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They held the arrested persons there, the arrested Croat soldiers and policemen. And there were also some criminals who were Serbs who had committed various offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about Croat civilians? Did you hear anything about them?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from the media, that those who were arrested were Croats. They were arrested during the exchanges. When they were talking about possible exchanges, then they were mentioning these arrested civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about a priest?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that one Catholic and one Orthodox priest were exchanged. Both of them were beaten up to quite an extensive degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Catholic priest was Croat, and the Orthodox priest was Serb?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that later, sometime in 1992. Then during those days, a lot of that was reported in the media during the trial. They also reported on it, and this is what brought it back in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session just a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we -- shall the Court please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzakula, given what -- given what you knew in 1991 about the SAO Krajina and about the war, do you have an opinion about whether -- whether you think Milan Martic would have, himself, been aware of those crimes that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness should tell us about what he knows personally. He should tell us whether he knows about certain things. As for his opinion and the question that was phrased in those terms by the Prosecution, I believe that that is completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the opinion I was seeking to solicit was -- and I tried to phrase it in the question was to be based on his knowledge at the time and facts. And I was going to of course clarify what -- if he had an opinion, what it was based on. And the Court could give it whatever weight it wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the phraseology was a little bit unfortunate, Mr. Whiting. I did note that myself, but I thought if the Defence was not going to object, I would let it go. But -- and I understood your use of the word "opinion" in context. However, given the objection, I think it would be advisable for you to lay the foundation for asking for that viewpoint on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to do that, Your Honour, but we'll see where this goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, during the war in 1991, you've already testified that you were living in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you follow the events of the war in the media?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did follow. We listened to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which media did you listen to? You've already spoken about different kinds of media. Can you tell us which media you listened to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed Zagreb and Belgrade media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you also have conversations with people -- and first I'm going to ask in 1991. Did you have conversations with people in 1991 about the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to people in my environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that environment include people who had spent time in the SAO Krajina during 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to 1991, then I can tell you that I spoke to Zecevic and Veselinovic. We spoke somewhere near Banja Luka in 1991. We just happened to meet there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, how about later? Did you -- after 1991, did you have further conversations with people about what had occurred in the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke in 1991 when I was in the government of the RSK, we spoke about what was going on in Western Slavonia, about the plight of our people, and what was happening in the villages there. I also remember when we travelled to New York, Mr. Zecevic and I. I spoke about Marrack Goulding, under-secretary of the UN. I spoke to him about the torching in Western Slavonia. And then he told me that in Dalmatia all Croatian villages had been razed to the ground. Then Stanko Zecevic told me about the combat that took place there, telling me that a lot of villages perished, a lot of civilians, soldiers and policemen were killed. At the time, after the government sessions, we did not go into detail. We did not discuss exactly what had happened. However, crimes were mentioned, especially the events of Milajcki -- of Miljacki plateau, or rather, Miljevac plateau, and other things that had happened there. We also asked for the trials to begin in Western Slavonia, for what had happened there. And in addition to that, we started setting up the judiciary. I remember that Mr. Ecimovic and I spoke to the judges who were supposed to conduct trials, and at the time they told us that they were not ready and that they could not put Serbs on trial. This surprised us. We said that it was not the Serbs who were put on trial, but rather certain individuals who had committed certain crimes. This indicated that people at the time were still not ready to take up such tasks. It was known that certain individuals had committed such acts. However, they were never tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you also in the media see -- were there reports that talked -- in 1991, were there reports that talked -- either in the Serb media or the Zagreb media that talked about Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was mentioned in the news. In Croatian media it was said that the Martic units, together with the JNA, were attacked in Croatian villages; whereas the Serb media spoke about the defence of the Serbian villages by the JNA and Serb TO and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified earlier that from February 1992 until about February of 1993, you were in -- you, yourself, was a -- you were in the RSK government, and Milan Martic of course was also in that government. Were you able then to observe Martic operating in the government and how he behaved with respect to his position?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He held quite a lot of authority in the government, both with respect to Zecevic and other ministers. He enjoyed a lot of respect, had a great authority among these people. He did not frequently attend government sessions, in view of his many obligations. He would usually be there when the first item was discussed, namely the military and political situation, and later on he would normally leave. However, he wielded a lot of authority, both when it came to his ministry, regarding which he proposed various regulations and so on, and it was never opposed, precisely because of his authority. He was supported by Rastovic, Bozanic, Zecevic, and I think that in that sense he had absolute authority as a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, do you know if the media that was available to you in Western Slavonia in 1991, was that also available in the Krajina region at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was possible to follow it because the areas are quite close and there was nothing to impede the broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've laid a foundation for the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, if I could go back to the question now. Do you think in 1991 that -- based on everything you know, do you think that Milan Martic would have known about the crimes that you heard about that were committed -- that you heard about being committed in the Krajina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was possible for him to know the SAO Krajina police could have informed him. He also could have received information through the media. As for Dalmatia, that was precisely the territory where he was most often present and, yes, he was able to know about the events that were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about Milan Martic at any time punishing or disciplining anybody for crimes committed against Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Prosecution put the penultimate question, I did not intervene, believing that that would complicate the situation further. I was going to object to the content of the questions. This question presupposes that there is an indisputable evidence of the crimes committed. We are now, in this trial, supposed to establish whether the crimes were committed, and if so, by whom and when. We are now dealing with the events reported by the media, and the Prosecutor now presents this in his question as evidence, as indisputable evidence that the crimes were committed and asks the witness to give his opinion. I believe that we are now on very dangerous ground, that jumps the gun, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I initially phrased -- I think you can see on the transcript that I said -- initially I did say: "The crimes that were committed," and then I rephrased it to say: "That you heard about being committed," and that was the point of the question. Does he think Milan Martic would have known about the crimes, that he heard about being committed. Of course I recognise -- the Prosecution obviously recognises that we have to prove that the crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. With your permission, I would like to say something briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My learned friend from the Prosecution first asked the witness about his opinion regarding that, whether it was possible for Mr. Martic to know that the alleged or actual crimes had, indeed, been committed. He asked the witness for his opinion, and then the next question was whether the witness knew that Mr. Martic punished somebody for the allegedly committed crimes. So we are now pre-empting the whole issue, and I believe that this is unacceptable. This question could be phrased in totally different terms, in a much more general way, which would not lead the witness to the answer. The Defence believes this to be extremely dangerous. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before I deal with the objection, can we get assistance. Our LiveNote are dead, and the record has now disappeared from the screen. I'm not able to bring it back to see what the witness has been saying. Okay. May I now deal with the objection. The problem I have, Mr. Whiting, with your question is that you put to the witness: "Did you ever hear about Milan Martic at any time punishing or disciplining anybody for crimes committed against Croat civilians?" That question puts into the mouth of the witness the -- the allegation that Mr. Martic did discipline or punish somebody. What you want him to answer is whether he did hear of that kind of punishment. In other words, you're stating it as a fact or it -- it is suggested to him that there has been a punishment and what is being sought of him is to say whether or not he heard of that punishment. Now, that, in my view, is leading; in other words, it's putting words into the mouth of the witness. And I think the question is objectionable, phrased in that sense. I think the question could be phrased differently so that we hear from the witness and not from counsel what, if anything, Martic did about these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. It certainly wasn't my intention to lead the witness, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that it may not have been your intention, but that is the result, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I try and intervene here maybe? I don't know whether this will help. Mr. Dzakula, do you know if anything happened to the people who allegedly committed the crimes that you heard anything about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear anything about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that disposes of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Dzakula, hear anything about what happened to people that committed other crimes, that is, crimes against Serbs? And here I'm talking about the time period of -- you can answer first for 1991, but then I'm going to ask you for the later time period.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether I heard about crimes against Serbs. I don't know in what sense do you mean? Serbs were killed in Croatia by Croatian side, and there were those who were killed by the Serbian side. And on the Serbian side, those who were suspected of the crimes were arrested and put in prison. When I was on the Serbian territory, when I was in the prison, I saw people who had committed crimes, killed other people, as a result of which they were detained in the prison in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who, to be clear, was detaining these people, that is, which entity or force in Glina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, police is the organ that arrests and detains people, and then once they are in prison, it is the investigative judge who conducts an investigation and issues indictments. So police was the organ which arrested people, and investigative judges did the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the people that you saw in the prison that you say were detained in the prison in Glina for having committed crimes, do you know if they committed crimes against Serbs or against Croats?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that I met there, that I saw there, were the cases where crimes were committed against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you aware of any crimes committed against Croats in Western Slavonia during 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of those crimes committed there in the territory of Western Slavonia in the north in Cetekovac, whereas in the Pakrac vicinity there were two specific crimes. A man called Sokolovic threw a hand-grenade, killing a whole family, and then a man called Kovacevic, nicknamed Sikirica, committed certain crimes with an axe. Initially he chopped down, with his axe, several Croats. And once there were no Croats, then he chopped down several Serbs. These were the most notorious crimes. These people moved about freely during the war. And once the Operation Flash was carried out, Kovacevic died in a clash with Croatian police, and Sokolovic drowned while fleeing across the Dravur [as interpreted] river into Bosnia. He couldn't swim. These people were never investigated or put on trial. Sokolovic, the person who committed this crime, occasionally went to Croatian side, across the confrontation line. Croatian police arrested and beat him, and during the beating he accused somebody else of the crime, falsely accused, and this person is now serving a 20-year prison sentence in Lepoglava prison, even though the crime was committed by Sokolovic and not the man in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These crimes that you talked about, the specific crimes that you talked about, when, to your knowledge, did they occur?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took place in early fall, in early October or late September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And these two men that you talked about, Sokolovic and Kovacevic, do you know anything about what they did from 1992 until Operation Flash in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokolovic was a member of the Territorial Defence; he stood guard. As for Kovacevic, I don't think he was mobilised. I think he was a civilian. I don't think anybody mobilised him. The other one I frequently saw in uniform bearing arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday about a Mirko Raskovic. Did you ever have a conversation with that man about Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak to him sometime in 1996 or 1997. We spoke even later. But then, in 1996 or 1997, we talked and mentioned Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was discussed in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I asked him, inter alia, whether he knew Milan Martic and he said that he knew him and that he personally replaced him or dismissed him from work. I don't know exactly whether he replaced him or dismissed him because he was harsh and violent in his demeanour, and that is why he was dismissed. I don't know which one of the two words he used, "removed" or "dismissed" from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know -- did he tell you when it was that he had either removed him or dismissed him from work, when that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was before the war. I don't know exactly which year. But at any rate, it was before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During 1991, did you hear about somebody by the -- that was referred to as Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard -- I heard about him. I read about him, heard about him over the media, the Serb media, about Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was referred to as a very capable officer who was familiar with military training, and that he was training soldiers who were called Knindzas, that he was doing that in the area of Knin, that his soldiers were brave, capable, courageous and that is the kind of thing that is written about what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yesterday you referred to the Posavina Corridor. Could you tell us what that is. What is the Posavina Corridor?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an area in Bosanska Posavina from Banja Luka. The area of Bosanska Gradiska, that part, to the border with Serbia. In that area, in Bosanska Posavina, there was a predominantly Croat population, although there were Bosniaks and Serbs, too. A road goes through it as a link between Krajina and Serbia. It had been blocked; that is the information that we received. And then the military forces of Republika Srpska and the military and police forces of the Republic of Serb Krajina wanted to make this break-through, so that the corridor would continue unhindered. The media were saying that there were no medicines for the hospital in Banja Luka and for children in Banja Luka, and other vital supplies were lacking and that is what was said at the time, that that is why it was necessary to create this passage, this corridor as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. It was the end of May/beginning of June 1992. I think it was sometime in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Martic played a role in that operation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Milan Martic led a unit from the Republic of Serb Krajina at this corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time it was mentioned at government meetings and also through the media, all the media. The success that was achieved through this break-through, Martic personally was promoted by the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina, Goran Hadzic, and the rank of general was bestowed upon him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, in your position in the government of the RSK, did you have occasion to see the signature of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, finally the moment we've all been waiting for. I'm going to try out the E-court system. Could we publish, please, 02076690.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, are you able to see that document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we supposed to do anything for that document to come on our screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the monitor, if you hit computer evidence, it will -- you'll see it in B/C/S. And on your own computer that you can log into, if you are in the E-court system, if you look at the -- if you've logged into English, you should see the English translation. And I don't know if the Court requires assistance for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We see the script -- the transcript. I see the ... You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I think in front of you you should see the second page of that document, in the bottom. Is that what you see?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise the signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the signature of Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There's also a stamp there. Are you able to say anything about that stamp?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a stamp of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd move this exhibit into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The exhibit is admitted into evidence. May it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be exhibit P11 -- Exhibits 7 to 11 have been assigned to the expert reports that were admitted by the Trial Chamber on the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now publish 02077288, please. Could we go to the last page of this document, please, on the -- only on the B/C/S. We can keep it on the first page for the English. And could we zoom in on the bottom half of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, are you able to recognise either of the signatures on this page?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise the signature of Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And which one is it? Is it the one on the right or the left?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right-hand side where it says "minister."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you say anything about the two stamps that appear on this document?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This stamp is the Republic of Serb Krajina, the Ministry of the Interior. This is a stamp of the ministry, and it looks like the kind of stamp that existed at that time in the ministries. And I assume that the other stamp is the stamp of the army of the Krajina of the Main Staff; that's what it says there. But the other one, the stamp of the Ministry of the Interior, is certainly the stamp of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document may be admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzakula, at the end of 1993, was there an election for president in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The election was held for the president of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who ran in that election?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic ran. I think that Babic ran, too, but Mr. Martic won the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic in -- during the campaign for the election, did Mr. Martic make speeches that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he went to different places and made election speeches. He had an election campaign going on. He was addressing the citizens of the RSK to support him in the election and to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall what positions he took in the campaign? What did he say his positions were in that campaign?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he talked about the state of the RSK, about the unification of the Serb lands, that is to say, uniting with Republika Srpska and Serbia. He often referred to Milosevic. He considered him the best and the greatest Serb politician. He said that Serbs should not be afraid, that they should vote in the election because there was a big struggle going on at the time, whether it would be Martic or Babic that would win the election. Both had their supporters. There were large-scale campaigns, but he primarily talked about uniting all the Serb lands. He also mentioned Karadzic and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he talk at all about Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I cannot really recall, because at that time I was not exactly moving about very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall -- were you able to tell if the media from Belgrade supported either of the candidates?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the media from Serbia thought that Milan Martic had an advantage, but a lot of people came, respectable people from Serbia, poets, writers - that's what I heard - friends, who came to support Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a clip of a speech by Milan Martic and ask you to watch it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have a transcript of this speech, which we'll distribute with the assistance of the usher. We also -- the transcript again will be played in a synchronised fashion on the clip. And I believe to watch this clip we have to switch to -- we should all be on computer evidence on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, were you able to watch and understand all of that clip that was played?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that speech or part of speech that we saw similar to the speeches that you testified about that you heard and saw during the campaign in 1993/1994?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd move this clip into evidence, the video clip and the transcript, as two separate exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the video clip be admitted into evidence as an exhibit together with the transcript -- or the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the transcript will be Exhibit P14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, in that speech there's a reference to a Mr. Macura. Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the founder of the Serb Democratic Party in Knin, and I think that he was the first minister of education in the government of the SAO Krajina, the one when Babic was prime minister. And he was loyal to Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1995, do you know if Milan Martic made any references to you in any speeches?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. When he was in Western Slavonia he said, among other things, that he has reserved space for Dzakula and various Dzakulas, and that he would put them into that room and never let them go. That was a threat addressed to me and people who thought what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear him say that yourself or did somebody tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that myself because I was nearby when this speech was being made. I was not in public; I was in a house and I watched this speech, I heard it. And later on I discussed it with my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did that occur, that speech?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Gavrinica in Pakrac. That is a settlement near Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when in 1995, if you can recall, did that occur?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime in 1995. I don't know if it was April or March. Sometime before Flash. That's when they came to see us to encourage us. And, among other things, Mr. Martic was talking about the highway, that it was opened at the time. He was saying that it was useless, and he attacked the fact that the highway was being opened. He said that we did not need oil and gas, that we could till the land with oxen. And he said that with our forces we would liberate all of Western Slavonia all the way up to Virovitica and let them just start. We're ready, he said. That was his speech of encouragement in this area to the people from that area. They did not believe him. After he left, I heard what people were saying. They laughed when this tilling the land with oxen was referred to. Because at least two or three years are needed for a cow to have a calf which would grow into an ox, and there weren't any oxen around. Oil and gas were important. And as for the war that he was praying for, people were precisely afraid of that, that that is what would happen, and that is indeed what happened later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In that last answer you made a reference to the highway being opened. Can you explain to the Chamber what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the area of Western Slavonia there is a highway, a road, between Zagreb and Belgrade. It used to be called the highway of fraternity and unity. It had been cut by the actions that took place during the war in 1991. And about 20 or so kilometres were under the control of the army of the authorities of the Serb Krajina. And at the end of 1994 or 1995, he was open -- the road was open for traffic, and it was used by Serbs and Croats and nobody was stopped there. And then at gasoline stations, people were able to get gasoline. And this was aimed at the normalisation of relations between Croatia and the Republic of Serb Krajina. There were people who were opposed to opening the highway, and there were other people who were in favour of it. Martic was among the people who was not in favour of that. The then-prime minister wanted the highway to be opened, and indeed he was the one who opened it. And later on it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, can you tell us what the Z-4 plan was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Z-4 plan gave a high degree of autonomy to the area that we called the RSK at the time. And different forms of that. The highest degree of autonomy with its own currency and flag was Banija, Kordun, Lika, and Dalmatia, and Western Slavonia was supposed to be integrated in the area of the Republic of Croatia and Eastern Slavonia. I think that it got a transition period of about five years for the process to develop. Quite a high degree of authority was given, great powers, and it was said then in the briefest possible terms that the Serbs in the area of SAO Krajina would have the status of a state within a state. The plan was written by international representatives, and it was represented by the four ambassadors, I think, of France, the US, Russia, and I can't remember who the fourth ambassador was who went to Zagreb and to Knin, advocating the adoption of this plan so that it could be put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in January 1995. It was mentioned a bit before that, too, and it was offered to the Krajina authorities in January 1995. I think it was January 1995, the end of January. And it was rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who rejected it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time the president of the republic, Mr. Martic, was being referred to. That -- he said that they could not receive the plan, let alone look at it and discuss it. And there were different thoughts whether the Krajina then -- some people were in favour of accepting it, whereas from the very outset Mr. Martic was against even receiving the plan, let alone adopting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, thank you very much. Those are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could this be a convenient moment then to take --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- our break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think so, and I think it's required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court will adjourn, and we'll reconvene at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Before I begin with my cross-examination, by your leave, Your Honour, I would like to give a brief information to you regarding the status of Defence at this point in time. Unfortunately, the Defence finds itself in the situation where lacks a lot of documents that it intended to introduce in the cross-examination of this witness. There is a simple reason for this. So far, the sum of 10 per cent, which was supposed to be paid into the account of the Defence before trial, has not been paid. I told you that we moved our office from Belgrade. A lot of our material, as I told you yesterday, has been placed in storage and we have no access to that material because we are unable to find ourselves an office here. I'm telling you this, even though I'm fully aware that this is not exactly the problem of the Trial Chamber; however, we are powerless to solve it in another way. We wrote to the registry on the 5th of January. We sent another information to them on the 12th of January, asking them to provide funds for us on that date so that we can set up an office here. Nothing has been done. It is uncertain whether it will be done at all. We are currently in hotel rooms, and we have with us the amount of material that we could store in hotel rooms. I apologise for bringing this up. I feel very uncomfortable about burdening you with these types of problems. However, it is questionable whether we can continue working in this trial. This is happening without any fault of ours. We did not contribute to this problem. We put in a lot of effort to ensure that the trial starts on time and to prepare for the cross-examination of this witness. I'm not referring just to the current situation, but I'm also speaking about the future situation, the future position of Defence in this trial. That's all I have to say on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Is there anybody in court here who represents the authority in the Tribunal who is responsible for making payments to the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honour? May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you may just hold on, Mr. Milovancevic. We're trying to get in touch with people who are responsible for this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to ensure that we understood each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understood each other, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to order that we take a short break for about ten minutes while this problem is being investigated, and hopefully the person responsible for solving the problem will be in court in ten minutes' time to give us an explanation. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 4.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van de Vliet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van de Vliet, the Chamber apologies for pulling you out of your work at this time of the day when you must be very busy, but we have a little hitch in the proceedings which we think you might be able to explain. The Defence is supposed to cross-examine the witness, and they indicate to the Chamber that they are not fully prepared to do so because they have not been able to set up an office. Their papers are still in storage, and this is because they have not received their first tranche of payment for the trial stage of this case. Are you able to give us an explanation as to why they have not been paid?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do my best in this short time frame that was given for me to prepare this. As far as I know and I've understood for now, the 10 per cent up front payment that we usually allow for Defence teams to start up their offices and prepare for trial has gone through our office but is now in the next office within the United Nations Tribunal system, which is the office of finance. To discover the exact details on where that is about, I will need more time, but it has been processed. As for the reasons, I think as you have probably seen previously, there has been an extensive debate with the Defence team about the level of complexity and the debate was only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. van de Vliet. We are aware of the extensive debate that took place in the pre-trial stage. We are now in the trial stage. Just before I continue, you are head of the unit, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the debate that raged about finances related to the pre-trial stage, the trial stage started on the 12th of December. The Defence should have had their 10 per cent before the 12th or December or just about that time to enable them to start the case. Now, you're saying that the processing of this payment has left your office and is in the finance section. When did it leave your office, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really can't give that level of detail at this moment. I really need to go back to the files and my staff, who has been dealing with this, to get all the details on dates, et cetera. I'm doing this on the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van de Vliet, you do appreciate that the Defence needs to have a fair trial, that the trial must go as expeditiously as possible, and that it is -- not only in the Defence interests, but it is in the interests of justice itself and in the interests of the public that the case proceed as expeditiously as possible, with minimum of interference with the Defence in its conduct of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That's what my office deals with on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I do not understand and the Chamber doesn't understand is why on the 17th of January, 2006, the Defence has not been paid their first tranche of the money when the trial started on the 12th of December, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask for a little bit of time and get back to you tomorrow with all the details that you need for this answer to be given properly and fully and completely, because I don't have the actual detail here with me. What I remember on the top of my head is that there was a debate on the complexity level also for the trial stage, which had to be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The debate on the complexity in the trial stage should not be the reason for non-payment. This trial -- this case had been put at level 2 for the pre-trial stage. There isn't any reason why there -- the Defence could not have been given 10 per cent of the level 2 level of the case while you determine whether it should shift from that level or not. And if it does shift from that level and it goes to level 3, all you need to do is to give the remainder of that. And if it does mean that it goes to level 1, then obviously you either call for the balance or you pay less for the next tranche. That should not have been the reason for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: I agree that there shouldn't have been a delay, and I apologise for that. As to the specific reasons, I really need to get back to my staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. van de Vliet. We -- this Court is going to convene most probably tomorrow for you to come and give us your explanations, but I would like you to remain in court in case we don't have to convene tomorrow so that you know exactly when we convene, because I'm going to ask the Defence a few questions to determine how this case is going to proceed from now on. And depending on that, I would like you to give that explanation at the next session of the case, okay? Please remain in court here while we ask the Defence. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, if you can answer me very briefly. Is the Defence in a position to proceed with the case right now or does the Defence need time to prepare?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we believe that at this point in time we can continue with work. The witness has been here for several days now, and we can continue the trial. We will do our best to represent the accused, Mr. Martic, in the best possible way. We can continue with the trial today, and that is my answer to the first part of your question. As for what is going to happen later on, that depends on how the developments evolve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I would like you to be very brief on your answer to my question. I do understand about the future, and I'm not talking about the future. What I do want to know, and I think it is in the interests of justice that the Chamber must know this, that you feel absolutely confident that with -- right now you are in a position to proceed and cross-examine the witness, you've got all the material that you need to cross-examine this witness, because the Chamber is concerned that justice not only be done but it must be seen to be done. Are you able to proceed now, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of the Defence team I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for putting this question to us. At this point in time, the Defence adapted all of its activities to the current situation. And in our view, we believe we can continue with this witness. Let me give you another brief explanation, with your permission. The Defence intended to tender into evidence some other documents which we do not have currently, but we hope that we will be able to tender them later on. That should not, however, affect the quality of our cross-examination. This means that we are doing the best we can in order not to interrupt the trial. That's what I wanted to say to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You must understand one thing, Mr. Milovancevic. The Chamber does not want the Defence to come back later and say: Had we been given an opportunity to prepare and prepare properly, we would have conducted our trial differently and now we have been prejudiced by that. And it is this prejudice that this Chamber is concerned to avoid. And therefore, the Chamber is not absolutely happy or not absolutely satisfied with your answer which says: Yes, but, because this is the effect of your answer. Yes, we are able to proceed, but we are inconvenienced because we don't have material to tender into evidence. We may tender it later. That's what I asked you to answer me very briefly and just a yes or no: Are you in a position to proceed with this trial, or are you not? And if you are not, and if you have any doubt that you are not in a position to proceed because you do not have all your documents, you must say so and this Chamber will give you an opportunity to get ready. Just please answer the Chamber definitively: Are you able to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. van de Vliet, you are excused from court. We are going to proceed. Will you be here, please, tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in this same court to give your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DE VLIET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are excused. You may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just raise one issue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First, I take the answer of counsel's -- I take -- I understand counsel's answers to mean that he will be able to start and complete the cross-examination without interruption, but that's obviously for the Court to determine. But the more important point that I wanted to raise was with respect to the next witness, and this is only because we need to prepare and be ready. So I'm just wondering if we can get some guidance about whether we -- it is still the intention to proceed with the next witness after this witness is completed or whether there's going to be a delay or a problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I think we heard what Mr. Milovancevic said. He says he doesn't know about the future, and of course he will not know about the future until OLAD has determined his future and how soon OLAD is going to determine his future, only OLAD knows. I do not think it would be fair to ask Mr. Milovancevic to give an indication about the next witness. Mr. Milovancevic has indicated that he is in a position to cross-examine this witness now. We shall take it one step at a time. And if he's able to carry on with the next, he will do so; if he's not, he will raise the point again and we decide it at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness please take the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You started testifying in this court about 1990, the events of that year, and this is what the Defence will be referring to initially. Did you explain here in the courtroom that in 1990 in Croatia the first multi-party elections were held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the full name of the then-Croatia at the time when these elections were held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us where these -- this Socialist Republic of Croatia was located in 1990.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to give us the full name of the country in which the Socialist Republic of Croatia was located.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Socialist Republic of Croatia was located in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as one of its federal units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, is it true that the Socialist Republic of Croatia was one of six federal units in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the inception date of the borders of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, the borders that existed when these first multi-party elections were held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These borders were set up during Avnoj conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you confirm that these borders of Croatia as one of the federal units date back to 1945, the end of World War II. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, in accordance with the constitution of Croatia at the time when the multi-party elections were held in Croatia, how many nations lived in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Croats, as a nation; Serbs; Slovenes; Macedonians; Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. My question was not specific enough. Can you please tell us out of these nations how many had the status of a nation according to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the Croats were a nation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were Serbs a nation in accordance with the constitution of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Serbs were a nation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. You told us that at the time when the first multi-party elections were held you were a member of a political party. Would you tell us what party?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to several months before the elections I was a member of the League of Communists of Croatia, and sometime just before the war broke out I stopped being a member. However, in the elections I voted for the League of Communists of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In order for the Trial Chamber and everybody else, including our colleagues from the Prosecution, to be able to follow, when you use the term "first multi-party elections," can you please tell us, prior to these elections how many parties, political parties, existed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just one political party, the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when the first multi-party elections were held in 1990 in Croatia, you were a member of the League of Communists of Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The League of Communists of Croatia, did it participate in those first multi-party elections under that name or did it have another name?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a new name. It was called the League of Communists of Croatia, the Party of Democratic Changes.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this mean that following the political developments in Croatia and in other republics, the League of Communists of Croatia changed its political image?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who was the chairman, who was the head of the League of Communists of Croatia Party For Democratic Changes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivica Racan was president or chairman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the nationality of Mr. Ivica Racan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was and still is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you, along with a large number of Serbs, voted for the Party of Democratic Changes, the party of Mr. Racan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the entire territory of Croatia, except for four or five municipalities, Serbs in the elections voted for the League of Communists of Croatia Party for Democratic Changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So can it be said that the Serbs in Croatia as a nation voting in the elections in the majority voted for the party led by Ivica Racan who was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. Since these were the first multi-party elections, can you tell us, if you remember, how many other political parties took part in the elections. Can you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can enumerate some, but maybe not others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest and the most important, the one that won was the Croatian Democratic Unity, led by Franjo Tudjman. Then there was the Croatian Party of Rights, Croatian Democratic Union, HSS --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it stands for, HSS?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian Peasants Party, then there was the Croatian People's Party, then there was Islamic Democratic Forum, then Islamic Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's quite enough, Mr. Dzakula. In addition to these parties, did the first -- did the Serbian Democratic Party take part in these first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian Democratic Party, which had been established in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the largest and most influential party was the Croatian Democratic Union led by Mr. Franjo Tudjman. Can you tell us when this party was founded?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this political party was founded in early 1990. It could have been February of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
