utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, am I right when I say that the HDZ was founded on the 26th or 28th February of 1989, whereas its first assembly as a political party was held in 1990 in the Lisinski Hall?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that first founding assembly of the HDZ which was held in the Lisinski Hall on the 24th or 26th of February, 1990? Do you remember any of the events at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Of all those parties whose names have been given, which one is the HDZ? We've had full names and suddenly we get "HDZ," and I don't know which of those parties is HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Croatian Democratic Union is known under the abbreviation "HDZ." This is an acronym in Croatian, in our language. Otherwise in English it's known as Croatian Democratic Union, CDU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the question I put to you. Do you remember the sentence uttered by Mr. Tudjman in the centre of Zagreb in late February 1990, prior to these multi-party elections, where he says - I'm going to quote his words - "The independent state of Croatia is not only a fascist creation and historical crime but also an expression of the historic orientation or attendances of Croatian people"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Following this founding assembly of HDZ, were the first multi-party elections held in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said something about the election campaign which was reported in the media. Can you please tell us what was the main slogan of this election campaign led by the HDZ prior to the elections?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they started displaying new flags. In the public it was known as the checker-board flag. They were chanting various nationalistic slogans. They said that Croats were subjugated by the Serbs in Yugoslavia, which was a prison for other nations, and that Serbs dominated the political scene and that that would have to change, that Croatia would become a national state of Croatian nation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did they mention that Serbs held key offices in the state administration, police, military, and so on? You mentioned something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were saying such things, that the Serbs predominantly held the most important offices in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Dzakula, that precisely at that time or right after that Stjepan Mesic was president of the Presidency of the SFRY, that is to say, the former Yugoslavia, the head of state?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mesic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. Let's not take up the time of the Court. Is it correct that the prime minister of the Yugoslav government at the time of these elections was a Croat, Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the minister of foreign affairs of Yugoslavia was a Croat, Budimir Loncar?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the minister of defence of Yugoslavia was Veljko Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: They say that one of his parents is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the commander of the air force, an anti-aircraft defence of Yugoslavia was also a Croat, Anton Tus, who after that crossed over to Tudjman's side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I'm sorry to -- I apologise for the interruption. I'm just wondering with this stream of questions whether we could have some indication of what time period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think at the beginning of his cross-examination Mr. Milovancevic indicated that he's dealing initially with the period 1990. Is that correct, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was putting these questions to the witness because I was talking about the time of the first multi-party elections, that is to say, April/May 1990. If that was not clear, I apologise to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, is it correct that the head of state security of Yugoslavia was Zdravko Mustac, also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the key people in the Yugoslav navy were Croats?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Admirals and generals?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time the commander of the 5th Military District was Konrad Kolsek, a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So that is the Zagreb Military District?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Dzakula, that the commander of the Belgrade Military District was General Spirkovski, Aleksandar Spirkovski, a Macedonian?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the assistant federal minister of defence of -- Mr. Kadijevic, that is, was also a Croat, Josip Greguric?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Josip Greguric was a Croat, an ethnic Croat?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll put another question to you in relation to these key offices. What about the deputy federal secretary of defence, that is to say, the deputy defence minister? Was it Stane Brovet, a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So can it be said that at the time when the Serbs in Croatia were accused of holding all key positions in the police, the army, the government, et cetera, the Yugoslav authorities were run by Croats from Croatia or were Croats by birth?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the election campaign was reported on in the Belgrade media, the Zagreb media, and all others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that everybody followed that campaign from the point of view of their own assessments, that is to say, Croats probably celebrated it and Serbs probably challenged it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a man with a great deal of experience born in the former Yugoslavia, can you confirm that as a rule young men from poor families joined the army and the police for the most part? Do you think that this is a possible assessment?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the military or the military academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the army. I'm talking about training for officers.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly people from poorer families went to train as officers because it was free of charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say whether it is possible to qualify the HDZ election campaign as a nationalist one when viewed from the point of view of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This election campaign, could it have realistically caused unrest or anxiety among the Serbs, and did it indeed lead to reactions on the part of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to put a question to you, and the Trial Chamber will judge whether it's acceptable. Have you ever heard of any such case in history, for example, when Jews were considered to be a factor of unrest and that they should be eliminated? I'm talking about Hitler's Germany.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these Jews, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to object to this line of questioning. I don't think it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any response to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm just trying to make a comparison of the political climates in two completely different periods of time. For example, the climate in the time of fascist Germany and the climate that was being created in a completely different time, and I'm trying to draw a parallel. What does that mean, when people belonging to one ethnic group or one religion or one race are being considered as if they had occupied everything and are holding all key positions. I have a very concrete context in mind when speaking of this. I do not intend to put provocative questions. My objective is to understand the positions involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear of the relevance of the question. I'm not quite clear how it will make you understand the positions involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to put another question. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. Thank you very much for -- are you now withdrawing that other question? Let's just get that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have withdrawn the question. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you explained that at these first multi-party elections which were held in April and May 1990, as a Serb in Croatia you voted for the Party of Democratic Change, the former communist party that was led by a Croat, Ivica Racan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained to us that many Serbs had voted for that party?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly why Serbs voted for that party. Do you see a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, throughout their history in Croatia, Serbs were always together with Croats in the HSS in the kingdom of the former Yugoslavia. They were anti-fascists during the Second World War, and they thought that at that point in time during these first multi-party elections the party of SKH, SDP would be the one that most lent itself for the building of a common future between Serbs and Croats in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could counsel please pause before putting his new questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Racan's party, the one that you voted for and that others voted for. Do you remember the vote that they won?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you make a comparison with the number of votes that was won by the Serb Democratic Party, the SDS, at those same elections when looked at Ivica Racan's Party of Democratic Change?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS won five seats, so there were five Serb MPs, and I think that in the SDP there were eight Serbs, perhaps even more than that. I don't know how many there were in other parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt, please. Mr. Milovancevic, you speak the same language as the witness, and there is interpretation taking place in between. Now, when you speak fast, the interpreter doesn't get the opportunity to interpret and you overlap with the witness and you are going to be missed. Now, I ask you to please slow down so that you give the interpreter an opportunity to interpret and the witness get an opportunity to answer. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do beg your pardon, Your Honours, and I do apologise to the interpreters as well. I am going to bear that in mind now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, is it correct that as a witness before this Court you stated that the Serbs in Croatia who at these first multi-party elections in Croatia voted for the Party of Democratic Change were disappointed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that that party did not bear their vital interests in mind. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat very briefly for us what the vital interests of the Serbs were at that point in time, in 1990, mid-1990, and immediately after that in the time of the multi-party elections in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost the Serbs expected that they would go on living in a common state, that is to say, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; that the Republic of Croatia would not secede from Yugoslavia; the Serbs expected that they would continue to be a constituent people; that the HDZ would not proclaim them a national minority by the new constitution; the Serbs expected that they would be protected rather than being dismissed from work just on account of the fact that they were Serbs. They were afraid and concerned because of the changes in the symbols of the Croatian state, the checker-board flag, which due to its legacy of the past caused a great deal of anxiety. And they thought that the Party of Democratic Change would offer some protection at the moment when the HDZ did not bear this in mind sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the Croatian Democratic Union, the party of Mr. Tudjman, at that time was it a majority party, and are you saying that it did not bear in mind these vital Serb interests?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this party, the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union and the parties that supported it in its policy, did it propose a change in the constitution of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croat Democratic Union propose and initiate a procedure for changing the constitution of Croatia in the following way: Serbs, according to this new constitution, would stop being a people and would be reduced to the status of a national minority?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Does it mean that once a people are a national minority they stop being people? That proposition put to the witness is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. The proposition put to the witness is: "Serbs, according to this new constitution, would stop being a people and would be reduced to the status of a national minority." Minorities are not -- national minorities are not people. Is that the insinuation? And if they are not people, what are they? Otherwise I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood me well, Your Honour. In the then-constitution of Yugoslavia, the state that was called the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there were six republics, according to the constitution. And every republic, say Macedonia, was predominantly the Republic of the Macedonian people; Slovenia was the Republic of the Slovenian people and of the other peoples living in it. So those peoples who, according to the constitution, were denoted as peoples. So it was only Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Macedonians, Bosnians that were peoples. Did I omit someone -- oh, yes, Montenegrins, sorry. Whereas all other ethnicities had the status of national minorities. Yugoslavia was well-known as a multi-ethnic community with over 20 national minorities living in it, but it is only the peoples who could have constituent significance. They were the only ones who could have a state. When saying "national minority," what is denoted is the members of a people who are a minority in Yugoslavia who have their own mother states outside the borders of Yugoslavia and who, because of that, on the territory of Yugoslavia have the status of a national minority but enjoy all human rights. That was a solution that was ensured by the Yugoslav constitution, the institution of Croatia, and the constitutions of all the other socialist republics, which, as federal units, comprised the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I perhaps take a simplistic view of the sentence. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honour, just one more sentence in addition to what I've already said in connection with your question. From a constitutional and legal point of view, it is only peoples who could express their views on their status within the Yugoslav community. They had legal standing. It's a complicated issue because only peoples could have republics as their own states. National minorities could not have that because national minorities have their own mother states. That's the explanation I was trying to provide. It's very complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Maybe you might try to provide that explanation via questions to the witness rather than testifying from the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when amendments to the Croatian constitution were being proposed, was there a deterioration in the status of the members of Serb people in Croatia in everyday life, in schools, health care, state administration, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there were certain disruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they start dismissing people from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were dismissed from work in the Croatian television company, various publishing companies. People were sent into early retirement within the police administration. The same applies to health care, education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These dismissals, were they based on ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who these people were who were dismissed at the time? You are talking about a phenomenon that existed then.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbs who were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could it be said that the Serbs were dismissed solely on the basis of their nationality? In other words, they were dismissed because they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us about the symbols used by the Croatian Democratic Union in their election campaign and later in political life. You said that this caused tension and anxiety among Serbs. Can you tell us more about this?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the Serbs were mostly upset by the checker-board coat of arms. The reason they were upset by this is that this symbol was used by the Independent State of Croatia between 1940 and 1945, which is a period of time when many crimes were committed against the Serb population. And this symbol brought back the memory of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned to you the speech given by Mr. Tudjman when he mentioned the Independent State of Croatia. Can you tell us what this state was, the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Independent State of Croatia was the ally of Hitler's Germany and Mussolini's Italy during the Second World War. It fought alongside with them against the countries such as Great Britain, Russia, France, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the assistance of the usher, please. Could we see Exhibit P3, which was shown to us yesterday. I hope you still have it. If not, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us the central portion where your finger is, this blue rectangle. All right. Thank you. Mr. Dzakula, in this white portion of the map in front of you -- yes, that's a perfect view. There in a small rectangle, what can we see there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. In that square we can see the former Yugoslavia. What is shown in this dark colour? Is it the territory of the Socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you move it to the left so we can see the green area, and could you please put it in the centre. Can you please read the heading that we can see in the upper right corner above that map.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I need my glasses. I need to bring it closer. "The map of Croatian genocide committed against the Serbs in the territory of the Independent State of Croatia between 1941 and 1945, committed by Ustasha forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. So this green colour on the map, does it show the territory of the Independent State of Croatia, mentioned by Mr. Tudjman in his speech of 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this map show the territory of Croatia shown in the dark colour plus the territory of neighbouring Bosnia and Croatia [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Above the map we can see -- or rather, below the map we can see a square, framed square.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the large green area that we see on the map is shown in this square as the territory which existed within the former Yugoslavia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Independent State of Croatia comprised the territory of the Socialist Republic of Croatia and the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the key, the map key, that we can see right below that map. What does it say in the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Localities where the Ustasha genocide was committed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is denoted with black dots?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The graves into which the Serbs were thrown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where this can be seen on the map. There are numerous such black dots. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And above that, above the key, we can see a red triangle. What does that denote?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wells into which Serbs were thrown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where these red triangles are? They are all over, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see a larger view so that it takes up the entire screen. And could you please centre it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the map key, Mr. Dzakula, is it true that all of these dots that we can see on the map are locations where crimes were committed, meaning that they are showing either the pits or the wells into which the Serbs were thrown?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us again during what period of time this happened and where.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took place between 1941 and 1945 during the existence of the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was in power at the time in the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were the members of his party called?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to this map. On the right of the map there is a text. I will read it out to you because the letters are very small. The text reads -- does it read as follows: "German general, Pilne Penetiary [phoen], in the Independent State of Croatia, Edmund Gleise von Horstenau, a historian by profession, writes that Ustashas claim that million of Orthodox Serbs were killed. Their throats were slashed, including women, children, and the elderly, and that according to him this represents an exaggerated boasting, because based on the reports received, the number of those whose throats were slashed amounted to three-quarters of a million, that is to say, 750.000 people." Is that what this text reads?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with these facts? You're a Serb from Croatia. You lived in Yugoslavia, just like all of us.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These facts were mentioned during the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did anything bad happen to your family in World War II?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Bad in the sense of what we just read out?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both villages -- or rather, residents of both villages, the majority of them, were killed. Ustashas threw the residents into wells. In one village, Kusonje, they set on fire the entire church full of people. Women and children were sent to Germany to labour camps, whereas my grandparents were sent to concentration camp in Jasenovac, Sisak and Stara Gradiska. This is where my parents also stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1942, August of 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please tell us in which state the majority of your relatives perished?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure -- it looks like we've gone for one and a half hours. Are we still okay in terms of our tapes, or shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I could take advantage of this moment to ask for a redaction just out of an abundance of caution, given the history with this witness. I would ask if we could redact page 62, lines 8 and 9, which potentially identify with a little too much specificity I think where the witness and his family is from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comment, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we mentioned only the area. And I don't think that redacting the text would change the essence. However, if the Chamber believes that this is necessary, we certainly won't object. I beg your pardon, if you believe that I went outside of what was the permitted area of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, just clarify on this issue because I think it might be -- this is the first time this has arisen. Just to be clear, when we're asking for a redaction, we're not asking that it be redacted from the transcript or from the official record, it's just that it not be broadcast to the public, and that is all we're asking. And to be clear, I'm not suggesting any criticism of Defence counsel. It arose in the natural course of questioning, and I'm just asking out of an abundance of caution that we redact it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure you would agree with that, Mr. Milovancevic? Okay. The redaction will then be made of -- the redaction of the question and the answer. But while we are on this pause, can I ask from the Prosecution: Are we likely to get an English translation of this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. That can be provided, Your Honour. We have that -- the version we have is, frankly, a little confusing, and I'd like to just make it a little more clear in terms of -- because it's difficult with the map where the translation pertains to, but that can be provided and we could provide that tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure the Bench will appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We left off when we were discussing the plight of the Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia. Can you please confirm that the majority of those who perished in the Independent State of Croatia were Serbs. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These people, did they die solely because of their ethnicity or was there any other reason?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Solely because of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We already said that the Independent State of Croatia was a quisling creation. It was a state that supported Hitler. We also mentioned General Horstenau as Hitler's emissary in that state. The map that we were discussing contains a number of facts that you confirmed to us. Mr. Dzakula, can you please tell us: Where did these victims end up? You told us that they perished because they were Serbs, and can you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the pits, wells. They were either burned alive in churches or their throats were slashed in churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the Independent State of Croatia that Croatian General Franjo Tudjman, the founder and the head of the Croatian Democratic Union, spoke about in his speech in 1990 at the founding assembly of the party?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Tudjman, as the person who said that this Independent State of Croatia is an expression of historic tendencies of the Croatian nation, did he also utter another sentence, and could you remind us of it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he was proud of the fact that his wife was neither a Serb nor a Jew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. In your testimony yesterday you mentioned General Spegelj. Can you tell us where he was a general, in which army, and what was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a general in the JNA, an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was he the commander of the Zagreb Military District?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the Trial Chamber. I am putting this question this way, but it is a generally known fact, so I have not made a mistake, Mr. Dzakula. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you saw a film about General Spegelj that my colleague from the Prosecution questioned you about yesterday or have you heard of that film?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched the film on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this film was shown, the one with General Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the beginning of 1991. Yes, it was in January, the second half of January 1991, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the content of that film? Why was it interesting? Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber and to us.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this film was shown and it showed how Mr. Spegelj was talking to some people and agreeing with them to kill some officers, and also he talked about arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what officers -- what officers would be killed? What is Mr. Spegelj saying in that film?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The killing of officers of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So that's the end of 1990 and beginning of 1991. Is that right? And the officer speaking is one of the top-ranking officer of the former Yugoslav People's Army, and he is talking about killing the officers of that same army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the film shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he was talking to, according to this film, judging by the film? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember now exactly who the man was that he talked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't insist on the details. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to put some questions to you, or rather, sentences that were uttered in that film. So could you please tell me whether they were actually said. Does Mr. Spegelj say on that occasion: "No, there is nothing for the army here. It will be completely destroyed. Five men cover each and every officer. We have to get rid of them physically." Somebody comes to the door. The door opens. Bang, bang, bang. Walks downstairs to another. "They should be killed on their own doorstep." Do you remember that kind of text from that film, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the sentence uttered by Mr. Spegelj: "Not a single officer will be permitted to reach the barracks, not a single one"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the following sentence: "The instruction is: Just take a pistol and right into the stomach"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: "That's going to be a war" -- sorry. Do you remember the sentence: "That's going to be a war, it's going to be a civil war. There will be no mercy for anyone, not even for women, children. Simply shells into family homes"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, was Mr. Spegelj shown on this film as a man saying: "We are going to solve the problem of Knin by a massacre"?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any mention in the film of the period of time or of the year when the film was made?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. Can you tell us who are these officers and soldiers who Mr. Spegelj is trying to kill this way?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officers and soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So at that time -- or rather, at that time was Croatia as a socialist republic part of the Yugoslav federation then?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no longer socialist, but it was part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army, did it exist as the federal armed force in every republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the JNA the regular army, a regular armed force?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did people of all ethnic backgrounds do their military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you know the reason why Mr. Spegelj was planning this? In what period did this happen, the end of 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of 1990/the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you of this. We were talking about the election campaign in the first half of 1990, the first multi-party elections in 1990, in May. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And who won in that election?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the basic political objective of this Croatian Democratic Union? What was their political objective?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political objective was an independent Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the objective to have Croatia secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why Mr. Spegelj was saying this, how officers of the federal army should be treated?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be taken as a conclusion, but I don't know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can withdraw the question. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the question's been withdrawn. It's very difficult with the pace to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Milovancevic, please try to slow down. Once again, I remind you that there's interpretation and you've got to give each other an opportunity to say and complete your sentences. If you will just bear that in mind, please. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll bear that in mind. I've already said that. Is it time to take a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to what I was told --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In another five minutes, I think, unless you're saying this would be a convenient time for you. Okay. It's going to be at --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree, Your Honour. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It will be then a 30-minute break. We'll come back at 25 to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We stopped when discussing the film about General Spegelj. In addition to what we've been saying until now, was there any mention of weapons in that film, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some weapons were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the film deal with the illegal import of weapons into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any mention of the quantity of weapons concerned?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mention that -- I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether after this film was shown any court proceedings were instituted against the persons mentioned in that film and that had to do with the illegal import of weapons into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Court proceedings were instituted in Zagreb, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these proceedings initiated in the first half of 1991 and were they brought to an end? Do you know that maybe?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the proceedings were instituted, but I don't remember that they were finished. I think they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzakula. ZNG, is that an abbreviation that means something to you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an abbreviation which fully means the National Guards Corps, Nacionali Zbor Garde [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can say that that is the embryo of the new Croatian army, a formation that was established by Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this new formation became well-known, when people heard of it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the beginning of 1991. I think that it was in Zagreb at a stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the stadium in Zagreb. What happened at the stadium then?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a review then, the first review of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the National Guards Corps an armed formation of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say in the first half of 1991, did the Yugoslav constitution state what the armed forces were and what they were made up of?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the only armed force was the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the constitution of Yugoslavia and according to the constitution of Croatia, was it possible within Yugoslavia to set up a new armed force, like the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know about these laws, I think that that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a question of a legal nature. At that time in Yugoslavia, were the only armed formations the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the HDZ, that is the Croatian Democratic Union, arming people, their own members, at the time? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit more about this.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I heard among the people was that the HDZ was arming itself, but I did not have any insight of my own, how and in which way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what period of time was the relevant period of time. When was this talked about? We are talking about 1990 and 1991. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this film that has to do with General Spegelj, the illegal import of weapons into Croatia is referred to. You said that the film talks about things that happened towards the end of 1990. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that these were weapons that were illegally imported towards the end of 1990 into the then-Republic of Croatia? Is that what the film refers to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the conclusion that may be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness answered the question before I had a chance to object, but maybe I'll nonetheless just object. I think that the -- that counsel is pressing the witness beyond what he heard to make comments of a legal nature or draw conclusions that he's really not in a position to draw. For example, were they illegal import. It wasn't clear to me whether the question was: Was that what he heard about on the tape, or is that his view, that it was illegal. And the same with respect to the question about armed formations, which the counsel phrased as a legal question. It seems to me that there's not a foundation for these sorts of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. -- that the question said: "Can it be said that these were weapons that were illegally imported towards the end of 1990 in the then-Republic of Croatia, is that what the film refers to?" Are you saying that the witness is not in a position to say whether the film refers to that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Of course, the second part of the question is a proper question. It's the first part of the question that -- I mean, there are actually two questions there, and it's the first question that I'm objecting to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the answer that was given, what does it answer to, the first or the second question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can't say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the counsel must carry the burden of his questioning. If he's going to put more than one question in one question and he gets an answer like that, he must argue at the end of the trial what that answer refers to. And if he doesn't clarify it, that's his problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say, Mr. Dzakula, that you heard that people were talking about the political party called the Croatian Democratic Union arming people. When did you hear that? From who? And who were these people?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where and who were they?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were they Serb eye-witnesses or can you tell us something a bit more about this, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I didn't ask them. It's just that these people said that they had heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the Serbs in Western Slavonia told you that the Croats were arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the order issued by the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Presidency of the SFRY, dated January 1991, saying that all illegally armed formations ought to be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any further details about what happened with that order? Was it implemented?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence, you mentioned a meeting in November of 1991 in Belgrade with Mr. Jovic and Mr. Milosevic. That meeting was held between them and the Serbs from Krajina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think that -- I think it misstates the testimony. I think it's 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was a meeting in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are we referring to the same meeting, namely the meeting where there were 20 to 30 Serbs, as you described, who came to Belgrade and met with Mr. Jovic and Mr. Milosevic where you encountered some opposition? When was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I apologise for the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say yesterday that you didn't know who exactly arranged this meeting, called for it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement given to the Prosecution, on page 20 it says that this was a meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. It's generally the practice at the Tribunal that when prior statements are put to the witness, that the witness is given an opportunity to see the statement in its language and look at it and have it before him. And I would ask that that be done in this case. I don't know if Defence counsel has a copy in the language -- I certainly have an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is certainly the understanding of the Chamber as the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if the witness may be given an opportunity to identify the statement as his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If he could be given a clean copy. I see the copy that's all marked up that's been provided. I have a clean copy of the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the misunderstanding. Thank you to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On -- in the -- on page 20, third paragraph from the bottom, this is the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in May of 2002. Does it state in that passage that you went to attend a meeting convened by Borisav Jovic, who was president of the Presidency of the SFRY; Slobodan Milosevic, who was the president of Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have trouble finding this passage that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry -- and I'm sorry to interrupt, but can counsel direct us on the English translation what page that appears? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me check. Just a moment, Your Honour. May I ask my learned friend from the Prosecution to give me the English version, because I'm unable to find it now and I don't want to waste any more time on this. And I believe that this would speed up the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, do you have an English copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do -- I was just checking if I had an extra one; I do. So I can provide this one to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's on page 18, the last paragraph. I just found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful to my learned friend, and I apologise to the Trial Chamber for this misunderstanding. I hope this will not happen again in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this third passage from the bottom, Mr. Dzakula, does it say that you went to attend a meeting organised by Borisav Jovic, president of the Presidency; Slobodan Milosevic, president of Serbia; and Ante Markovic, president of the Federal Executive Council, which is to say the federal prime minister?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say in the same paragraph that the meeting was convened in order to clarify the status of Serbs in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a mistake. That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify? What is this mistake about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just the status of Serb in Western Slavonia, but rather the status of Serb in Croatia, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When giving evidence and answering questions from the Prosecution yesterday, did you speak about the fears --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to object because the -- what is said in the paragraph has been misstated. It does not say that the meeting was convened in order to clarify the status of Serbs in Western Slavonia. What it says is: "I went to a meeting organised by these people to explain the position of Serbs in Western Slavonia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, on page 18 of the English translation in the last paragraph it says that this was in November 1990, and now I'm reading the text where the witness says: "When I went to a meeting organised by Borisav Jovic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Ante Markovic to explain the position of Serbs in Western Slavonia." I quoted this text, but uttered it in the language of the witness. And I don't understand. What is the objection of the Prosecution? I'm unaware of having made any mistake; therefore, I do not understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, does the statement in the language of the witness say that the meeting was called or convened in order to clarify the status of Serbs, or does it say that the witness attended the meeting in order to explain the status of the Serbs? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will read out verbatim the text that was sent to us, the translation of it. Can I do that? Can I read it out now? The entire text of this passage reads as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like -- the Court would like you to read the original text that was written by the witness. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Association of Serbs from Croatia was founded by certain Serbs from Croatia living in Belgrade. I met with them in November 1990 when we went to a meeting organised by Jovic, Milosevic, and Markovic to clarify the position of Serbs in Western Slavonia." Further, the text reads: "We did not meet with Markovic. First we met with Borisav Jovic. Some other people from the Knin area came as well. They were euphoric and spoke about persecutions of Serbs in Croatia. The rest of us were not given opportunity to speak." Therefore, my question to the witness pertained solely to this portion of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the original is, in fact, the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much to the interpreters. You heard that, Mr. Milovancevic. Apparently the original text is the English version. So that which you are reading is a translation, in which case I must apologise to you and ask that the English version, which is now said to be the original, be the one read. Let's hear what it says and then we'll find out from the witness what he actually said in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The Association of Serbs from Croatia was established by some Serbs from Croatia living in Belgrade. I met with them in November 1990 when I went to a meeting organised by Borisav Jovic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Ante Markovic to explain the position of the Serbs in Western Slavonia. We did not meet with Mr. Markovic. We first met with Mr. Borisav Jovic. Some other people from Knin region came there as well. They were euphoric and talked about persecutions of Serbs in Croatia. The result of us -- the rest of us could not get the opportunity to speak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There maybe some ambiguity in that statement. And I'm not quite sure whether you want to get it clarified by the witness, or do you want the Chamber to try and say what the ambiguity is at this stage? I'm reluctant to say the ambiguity until we hear the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, I simply want to show to the Trial Chamber what our intention was. It was not my intention to quote the text verbatim. I was more relying on the content and the essence of it. I wanted to ask the witness whether he attended the meeting, and if so, who convened it. And then I wanted the witness to tell us in view of these two texts whether it was true that Ante Markovic was one of the persons convening the meeting. At the time, Ante Markovic was president of the Federal Executive Council; he was federal prime minister. I'm not here to harmonise the two texts. I'm simply here to put a question to the witness based on the texts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That may very well be so, Mr. Milovancevic, and I think you will still have the opportunity to do so. However, an objection has been raised by your learned friend on the opposite side based on a specific question that you asked. You asked him the question: A meeting had been convened in order to explain the position of the Serbs. The objection says: No, that's not what the statement says. The statement says: "I went to the meeting in order to explain the position of the Serbs." Now, in view of the objection, notwithstanding your good intentions, I think we need to clear that little misinterpretation or misunderstanding, and I think the witness should be asked to clarify in a point: What is it that actually happened? Did he know the purpose of the meeting to be -- to explain the status of the Serbs? Or did he go to the meeting with the intention of explaining the status of the Serbs? Can you clarify that question, please, and then you can go to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, just one sentence. I would like to point out one thing to the Trial Chamber. The original text is in English; however, the original statement is the one that the witness gave in his native language. He didn't give his statement in English. He gave it in his native language and then that was translated into English. Perhaps the easiest thing to do would be to ask the witness why he went to this meeting and to have him explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, were you present when the witness wrote the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I understand what you're asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you can't tell us in what language he made the statement, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is here, he can clarify all these questions. So stop testifying from the bar. Let the witness clarify the issues that I've asked you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It wasn't my intention to create further misunderstandings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please clarify the issue with the witness, otherwise the Court will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzakula, did you attend the meeting in Belgrade in November of 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it came about that you came to the meeting and what was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by my colleague, a member of the Regional Board of the SDS for Western Slavonia, Slavko Lukic, that there would be a meeting in Belgrade attended by representatives of Serbs from Croatia. He said it would be very important for me to attend as well. He was unable to tell me where the meeting would be held and with whom. I headed out to Belgrade with him. I was told that he would be told this en route, and I was told that it would be good for me to be present. So I travelled with him, and when we arrived in Belgrade we met with the representatives of the Serbs from Croatia. That was the first time I met them. It was then that we were told that a meeting would be held with Ante Markovic, president of the Federal Executive Council; Borisav Jovic, president of the Presidency of the SFRY; and Slobodan Milosevic. However, the meeting was held only with Borisav Jovic, in his office, and later on in Slobodan Milosevic's office. Ante Markovic did not see us. Therefore, I didn't know who convened the meeting, nor did I know where the meeting would be held until I arrived in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the Court is going to clarify the question for you because you are not clarifying the question. Mr. Dzakula, when you went to this meeting, did you know the purpose of the meeting; and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was said that we should give our opinion about the problem and the position of Serbs in Croatia and their sentiments. I went to the meeting intending to speak about Western Slavonia, which I was familiar with, and I wanted to use this opportunity to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I repeat the question, Mr. Dzakula. When you went to the meeting, did you know why the meeting had been convened, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you went to the meeting, did you have any purpose of your own? What was the reason you went to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I heard that there would be a large group from Croatia going to the meeting, I wanted to be informed. I wanted to hear what was going to be discussed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is -- was that all you wanted to do at the meeting, to be informed about what is discussed there? Or did you have any other reason for going to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wanted to see what was going to be discussed there; and then if the meeting went into the problems concerning Western Slavonia, I was going to use that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To use the opportunity to do what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To speak about the situation in Western Slavonia, to discuss whether there were any problems and what kind of problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was that all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzakula. I think the witness has cleared the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just take note of the hour. I don't know if the Court has lost track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It is past 7.00, Mr. Milovancevic. Is it convenient or do you want to round off a point before we close?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. [Interpretation] I think that this will do for the time being. We can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Court will adjourn to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.09 p.m.,
